newsitem.title: USA: Civil rights leader Lowery gives farewell speech.
newsitem.headline: Civil rights leader Lowery gives farewell speech.

text.p: In a farewell address to the organisation he founded with Martin Luther King Jr., retiring Southern Christian Leadership Conference president Joseph Lowery on Monday defended affirmative action and called for more help for inner cities.

Lowery is stepping down after 20 years as head of the civil rights organisation. His successor was to have been elected this week, but Lowery was asked on Monday to remain as SCLC president for three to six more months.
"Where do we go from here? Activism," Lowery told an overflow crowd at Ebenezer Baptist Church on historic Auburn Avenue. "Where do we go from here? Unity."

"We must stand firmly by affirmative action," he said. "When the government by public policy kept you out, the government has a responsibility by public policy to bring you in. And it needs to be just as intentional about including you as it was about excluding you."

The 75-year-old Lowery, who led many civil rights marches through the South, called on President Bill Clinton to provide more resources to the nation's cities. "There is no way under God's sun to deal with racism and the complexities and the crises around race without dealing with the inner city," he said.

"How are you going to deal with drugs and crime and despair and frustration without dealing with the city?" Lowery asked. "I know you can't solve all the problems with money, but I guarantee you can't solve many without it."
Lowery was to have retired this week, but the civil rights organisation's board members agreed on Monday to delay the election of a new president.

"They just haven't settled on a candidate," SCLC spokesman Deric Gilliard said. "They have asked Dr. Lowery to stay on for 90 days because they want to be sure. The maximum would be until Dr. King's birthday of January 15."

As part of events marking the SCLC's 40th anniversary, Lowery was honoured on Sunday night with a gala tribute attended by the Rev. Jesse Jackson, King's widow, Coretta Scott King and former United Nations Ambassador Andrew Young.
